text: Standard Linux permissions are Discretionary Access Control, or DAC — access decided at the file owner's discretion, and root bypasses those checks entirely. Mandatory Access Control adds a second, system-wide policy layer on top of DAC that even root can't opt out of. The two major real-world Linux MAC implementations are SELinux and AppArmor, and they take genuinely different approaches to enforcing that same idea.

SELinux, the NSA-developed default on RHEL, CentOS, and Fedora, attaches a security context, user:role:type:level, to every process and file. Policy decides which process types can touch which file types, independent of normal permissions. Check the current mode with getenforce or sestatus, and switch it with setenforce — 1 for enforcing, which blocks and logs violations, or 0 for permissive, which only logs them for testing.

AppArmor, the default on Ubuntu, Debian, and SUSE, skips labeling altogether. Each confined program gets a plain-text profile in /etc/apparmor.d/, named after its binary path, listing exactly which files it may read, write, or execute. aa-status shows what's loaded; aa-enforce and aa-complain switch a profile between blocking and log-only testing. It's generally easier to read at a glance than SELinux's label-and-policy model.

Here's why that second layer matters: an attacker drops a web shell through a vulnerable upload form, getting code execution as the apache user. DAC passes immediately — apache owns the web root. But SELinux's httpd_t policy never grants that process type access to /etc/shadow or a raw socket, so the breach stays contained to web content, regardless of what DAC alone would have allowed.

That containment happens automatically, whether or not the compromised application was ever coded to check for it — which is the entire point of a mandatory layer sitting above ordinary file permissions, enforced the same way for every process on the box. Next up: auditd, the Linux audit subsystem that logs security-relevant activity at the kernel syscall level, catching things an application's own logs can miss entirely.
